item.title: Fool the Lockout
item.description:
Fool the Lockout

Category: Web | difficulty : Medium | platform : PicoCTF

Problem: The challenge is a login web page with faulty rate-limiting logic. We’re given a leaked username;password list and expected to brute-force the login while bypassing the rate limit.

Solution in one line: Stay just under the server’s max-requests-per-epoch threshold by pacing requests evenly within each window, so the lockout condition is never triggered.

Concepts: rate-limit bypassing brute-forcing python scripting

item.title: SSH Auth Failure Diagnosis — Kali Linux VM
item.description: PROBLEM > SSH from my NixOS host into a Kali VM. Should’ve taken thirty seconds. Took an hour.

Passive Recon Case Study — RBB Bank Phishing Kit (Firebase + Vercel)

Date: August 2026
Target: rastriya-banijya-bank.web.app / rastriya-banijya-bank.firebaseapp.com
Assessment Type: Passive Reconnaissance (non-intrusive)
Supporting Files: raw_output.json, report.md

Overview

This case study documents the passive reconnaissance of a phishing site impersonating Rastriya Banijya Bank (RBB), a Nepali government-owned commercial bank. The site was discovered in the wild hosted at:

  • rastriya-banijya-bank.web.app
  • rastriya-banijya-bank.firebaseapp.com

The phishing kit impersonates RBB’s KYC update portal, luring victims with a fake “KYC re-verification” prompt. This is consistent with a documented fraud campaign — RBB issued public warnings in October and November 2025 about fraudulent KYC-update links exploiting the Gen-Z protest aftermath in Nepal. The lure preys on urgency and trust: users believe their bank account will be suspended unless they “re-verify” their identity through the provided link.

item.title: Recon Tool
item.description:
Building a Passive Recon Tool to Understand Web Security Better

System backend is a vast topic. No two applications share the same mechanism, let alone the same backend. Each one has its own architecture, security posture, and weak points. The more we understand a system’s backend, the more we start to see how its security holds up, things like header policies, TLS configuration, DNS hygiene, and what information it leaks publicly.
